# Organizing finite element operations with functions {#sec-two-springs-functions}

::: {.callout-important}
## Task: Organize the FEM operations into functions

Refactor the two-spring script so that its main finite element operations are
implemented as Julia functions, while preserving the existing finite element
calculation and numerical results.
:::

## Starting point

In @sec-two-springs-code, the direct stiffness procedure was translated into the
first MiniFEM Julia script. The resulting program is intentionally explicit: the
input data, element operations, assembly, boundary conditions, solution, and
post-processing all appear directly in the top-level script. This makes the
numerical procedure easy to follow line by line. However, several parts of the
program now represent well-defined operations that can be given names of their
own. For example, the element stiffness matrix is constructed directly inside
the element loop:

```julia
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
```

Similarly, global assembly, force assembly, application of the displacement
constraint, and strain-energy computation are all written directly where they
are used.

We will use the final code from the previous snapshot as our starting point and
[refactor](../glossary.qmd#gls-refactoring) its implementation without changing
the finite element calculation.

## Goal of this snapshot

The goal of this snapshot is to refactor the existing two-spring program using
Julia functions.

The mechanical problem, finite element formulation, input data, boundary
conditions, and numerical results will remain unchanged. The implementation will
be reorganized into functions, and some diagnostic output will be simplified.

By the end of the snapshot, the following finite element operations will have
their own functions:

```text
spring_stiffness
assemble_stiffness!
assemble_forces!
apply_homogeneous_constraints!
strain_energy
```

The top-level part of the script will then describe the overall finite element
workflow by calling the higher-level functions, while `assemble_stiffness!` will
use `spring_stiffness` internally.

The refactored program must reproduce exactly the same numerical results as the
starting snapshot. We will verify this after completing the refactoring.

## From operations to functions

The syntax for defining and calling Julia functions was introduced in
@sec-julia-defining-functions. We now apply those ideas to the existing
two-spring implementation.

Our approach will be incremental. For each finite element operation, we will
first identify the corresponding block of code in the starting snapshot and move
that code into a function with as little modification as possible. We will then
replace the original block with a call to the new function. We will consider
further improvements to the function only after this direct extraction.

Two types of functions will appear in this snapshot:

- functions that compute and return a result;
- functions that modify an existing object supplied as an argument.

The distinction will become clear as we refactor the code.

As each function is introduced below, place its definition before the top-level
pre-processing section. The finite element functions will therefore remain
grouped together, followed by the top-level analysis that calls them.

Variables introduced inside the extracted functions are local to those
functions, following the function-scope rules introduced in
@sec-julia-defining-functions. This allows each operation to manage its own
temporary quantities without exposing them to the top-level analysis.

## First step: extract the element stiffness operation

A useful way to introduce functions into an existing program is to begin with a
small, self-contained operation.

In the previous snapshot, the element stiffness matrix is constructed inside the
element loop:

```julia
k_e = element_stiffness[e]
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
```

The matrix construction depends only on `k_e`, so it can be moved directly into
a function, as shown below.

*Before*

```julia
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
```

*After*

```julia
function spring_stiffness(k_e)
    K_e = [
        +k_e -k_e;
        -k_e +k_e
    ]
    return K_e
end
```

Place this function near the beginning of the file, immediately below the
descriptive comment in the file header.

The original matrix construction inside the element loop is then replaced by

```julia
K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)
```

Nothing has changed mathematically. The same value of `k_e` produces the same
matrix `K_e`: the operation has simply been given a name.

This is the first type of function introduced above: `spring_stiffness` receives
the data required for the calculation and returns a new result. It does not
modify `k_e`.

This first transformation illustrates an important refactoring principle used
throughout this snapshot:

> first move an existing operation into a function without changing how the
> operation itself is performed.

Once the function works, its interface can be considered separately.

Before attempting the next refactoring step, run the program and confirm that it
produces the same numerical results as before.

## Extracting global stiffness assembly

The next operation is larger. After extracting the element stiffness operation,
global stiffness assembly is still performed by the complete element loop:

```julia
for e in 1:num_elements
    # Element stiffness matrix: K_e = k_e * [1 -1; -1 1]
    k_e = element_stiffness[e]
    K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)

    println("\n-- Element ", e, ", k_e = ", k_e)
    println("   Element stiffness matrix K_e:")
    display(K_e)

    # Map local DOFs to global DOFs for an element:
    # the local to global DOF mapping is built from element nodes
    # through the element connectivity matrix (for elements with one DOF
    # per node, the global DOF is the same as the node number).
    dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

    # Assemble the local stiffness matrix into the global stiffness matrix.
    for i in 1:2
        I = dof_map[i]
        for j in 1:2
            J = dof_map[j]
            K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
        end
    end
end
```

At this stage, keep the loop unchanged and place it inside a function:

```julia
function assemble_stiffness!(
    K,
    element_connectivity,
    element_stiffness,
    num_elements,
)
    for e in 1:num_elements
        # Element stiffness matrix: K_e = k_e * [1 -1; -1 1]
        k_e = element_stiffness[e]
        K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)

        println("\n-- Element ", e, ", k_e = ", k_e)
        println("   Element stiffness matrix K_e:")
        display(K_e)

        # Map local DOFs to global DOFs for an element:
        # the local to global DOF mapping is built from element nodes
        # through the element connectivity matrix (for elements with one DOF
        # per node, the global DOF is the same as the node number).
        dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

        # Assemble the local stiffness matrix into the global stiffness matrix.
        for i in 1:2
            I = dof_map[i]
            for j in 1:2
                J = dof_map[j]
                K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
            end
        end
    end
end
```

The original element loop can now be replaced by

```julia
assemble_stiffness!(
    K,
    element_connectivity,
    element_stiffness,
    num_elements,
)
```

Again, the assembly algorithm itself has not changed. The nested loops, the
local-to-global map, and the additive update of `K` are exactly the operations
used in the previous snapshot.

Unlike `spring_stiffness`, this function does not construct and return a new
global matrix. It modifies the existing matrix `K` through the accumulated
assignment

```julia
K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
```

For this reason, the function is named `assemble_stiffness!`. As introduced in
@sec-julia-defining-functions, the trailing `!` is a Julia naming convention
used to signal that a function modifies one or more of its arguments; the `!`
does not itself cause the modification.

## Choosing function arguments

The first version of `assemble_stiffness!` reproduces the existing assembly
operation with as little modification as possible. We can now move from direct
extraction to a small refinement of its interface by inspecting its arguments.

The function currently receives

```julia
num_elements
```

but the number of elements can already be determined from

```julia
element_connectivity
```

using

```julia
size(element_connectivity, 1)
```

Passing both pieces of information creates unnecessary duplication. To remove
this redundancy, move the calculation

```julia
num_elements = size(element_connectivity, 1)
```

inside the function:

```julia
function assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)
    num_elements = size(element_connectivity, 1)

    # element loop
end
```

The call then becomes

```julia
assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)
```

and the top-level definition of `num_elements` is no longer required.

This gives a useful guideline for designing function interfaces:

> pass the information required to perform an operation, but avoid passing a
> quantity that can be obtained unambiguously from information already available
> to the function.

This is a guideline rather than an absolute rule. Later implementations may make
different choices for reasons of efficiency or software design.

## Keeping numerical operations separate from printed output

The first extracted assembly function still contains the diagnostic output from
the starting script:

```julia
println("\n-- Element ", e, ", k_e = ", k_e)
println("   Element stiffness matrix K_e:")
display(K_e)
```

These statements were useful in the first snapshot because the intermediate
element matrices were deliberately exposed while introducing assembly. The
purpose of `assemble_stiffness!`, however, is to perform the numerical assembly
itself. Displaying intermediate results is a separate task: it does not
contribute to the assembly operation and need not be part of the function.

You can therefore remove these three statements from `assemble_stiffness!` and
let the top-level script report the beginning and result of the assembly
operation:

```julia
println("\n- Assembling local stiffness matrices into global K")
assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)

println("\n- Global stiffness matrix K:")
display(K)
```

The numerical calculation has not changed; only the diagnostic output produced
inside the assembly loop has been removed. This keeps the numerical operation
separate from the decision about what information should be displayed to the
user.

This is an example of [separation of
concerns](../glossary.qmd#gls-separation-of-concerns): the numerical function is
responsible for performing the assembly, while decisions about diagnostic output
are kept outside the function.

## Extracting force assembly

The applied nodal forces are still assembled directly in the top-level script:

```julia
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
```

This is already a small, self-contained operation.

Move it directly into

```julia
function assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
    for (dof, value) in applied_forces
        f[dof] += value
    end
end
```

and replace the original loop with

```julia
assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
```

The function modifies `f`, so its name follows the `!` convention.

Notice also that the function does not need to know anything about springs. It
only receives a global force vector and a collection of degree-of-freedom/value
pairs.

This is the first indication that some of the operations being extracted from
the two-spring example are more general than the particular mechanical problem
that introduced them.

## Extracting the displacement constraint

The homogeneous prescribed displacement is still imposed directly in the
top-level script:

```julia
for dof in constrained_dofs
    for i in 1:total_dofs
        K[i, dof] = 0.0
        K[dof, i] = 0.0
    end

    K[dof, dof] = 1.0
    f[dof] = 0.0
end
```

As before, begin with a direct extraction:

```julia
function apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
    total_dofs,
)
    for dof in constrained_dofs
        for i in 1:total_dofs
            K[i, dof] = 0.0
            K[dof, i] = 0.0
        end

        K[dof, dof] = 1.0
        f[dof] = 0.0
    end
end
```

The original loop can then be replaced by

```julia
apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
    total_dofs,
)
```

The function modifies both `K` and `f`, which again motivates the trailing `!`.

### Refining the arguments

As with `num_elements` in the assembly function, one of the arguments can be
obtained from information already available to the function.

The number of global degrees of freedom is equal to the number of rows of `K`,
so it can be determined directly from the matrix:

```julia
total_dofs = size(K, 1)
```

There is therefore no need to pass `total_dofs` as a separate argument. Move
this calculation inside the function.

The function definition therefore changes from

```julia
function apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
    total_dofs,
)

    # constraint loop
end
```
to

```julia
function apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
)
    total_dofs = size(K, 1)

    # constraint loop
end
```

and the corresponding call becomes

```julia
apply_homogeneous_constraints!(K, f, constrained_dofs)
```

Unlike `num_elements`, the top-level variable `total_dofs` is still required
elsewhere in the script to initialize the global arrays:

```julia
K = zeros(total_dofs, total_dofs)
f = zeros(total_dofs)
```

It therefore remains part of the pre-processing stage. The `total_dofs` defined
inside `apply_homogeneous_constraints!` is local to that function and is
separate from the top-level variable with the same name.

## Extracting the strain-energy computation

The global strain energy is still computed directly in the top-level script:

```julia
strain_energy_global = 0.5 * transpose(u) * K_original * u
```

Extract this operation into a function that receives a stiffness matrix and a
displacement vector and returns the corresponding strain energy:

```julia
function strain_energy(K, u)
    return 0.5 * transpose(u) * K * u
end
```

and replace the original expression with

```julia
strain_energy_global = strain_energy(K_original, u)
```

The analytical reference calculation remains in the top-level script because it
is specific to the two-spring benchmark:

```julia
k_1 = element_stiffness[1]
k_2 = element_stiffness[2]
strain_energy_analytical =
    0.5 * applied_force^2 * (1 / k_1 + 1 / k_2)
```

The same applies to the analytical displacement vector:

```julia
u_analytical = [15.0, 0.0, 10.0]
```

These quantities are used to verify the finite element solution rather than to
define reusable finite element operations.

Before finishing the refactoring, clean up the comments so that they describe
the new program structure rather than the original top-level implementation.
Update headings and descriptive comments where necessary, add concise comments
for the new function block, and remove comments that have become redundant.
These changes affect the documentation only, not the executable code.

## Structure of the refactored program

The mathematical sequence of the program has not changed. The main difference is
that several finite element operations now have explicit names:

```text
Pre-processing
    define model data
    initialize K and f

Processing
    assemble_stiffness!(...)
    preserve K_original
    assemble_forces!(...)
    apply_homogeneous_constraints!(...)
    solve K * u = f

Post-processing
    strain_energy(...)

Verification
    compare with independently derived reference results
```

The resulting top-level script exposes the overall finite element workflow,
while the implementation of individual operations is contained in separate
functions.

@fig-s02-program-structure shows how the top-level script delegates individual
finite element operations to the functions introduced in this snapshot.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-s02-program-structure
%%| fig-cap: >-
%%|   Function-call structure of the refactored two-spring program.

flowchart TB
    TOP["Top-level script"]

    ASSEMBLY["assemble_stiffness!"]
    FORCES["assemble_forces!"]
    BC["apply_homogeneous_constraints!"]
    ENERGY["strain_energy"]
    ELEMENT["spring_stiffness"]

    TOP --> ASSEMBLY
    TOP --> FORCES
    TOP --> BC
    TOP --> ENERGY

    ASSEMBLY --> ELEMENT
```

## What changed?

The finite element procedure itself has not changed. What has changed is where
the details of each operation are expressed.

In the starting snapshot, the top-level script describes directly *how* an
operation is performed. For example:

```julia
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
```

After refactoring, the top-level script instead states *what* operation should
be performed:

```julia
assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
```

The implementation has not disappeared; it has moved into a named function.

The same transition has been made for stiffness assembly, application of the
homogeneous constraints, and strain-energy computation. The top-level script
therefore exposes the finite element procedure more clearly, while the detailed
implementation remains available in the function definitions.

## Verification after refactoring

Refactoring should not alter the numerical problem being solved.

Run the modified program and verify that the assembled stiffness matrix is still

$$
  \mathbf{K}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2 & 0 & -2\\
  0 & 1 & -1\\
  -2 & -1 & 3
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{N/mm}.
$$

Before displacement constraints are imposed, the matrix should remain symmetric
and each row should sum to zero, reflecting the rigid-translation mode of the
unconstrained assembly.

The displacement vector should remain

$$
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  15\\
  0\\
  10
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm},
$$

and the numerical strain energy should remain

$$
  U=75\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
$$

## What comes next

The finite element operations are now represented by individual functions, but
the overall analysis is still executed by top-level statements in the script.

The next snapshot will use these functions to make the complete two-spring
analysis callable as a single operation. This will provide a natural interface
for running the same analysis from other Julia code and, subsequently, for
automated regression testing.

For now, the **explicit top-level operations → named finite element functions**
transition is complete. The finite element mathematics has stayed the same while
the program has become more structured and reusable.
